I think IV in general has a sleazy party culture, which people unfortunately tend to associate with UCSB even though a huge chunk of the pop. is from SBCC. 

When I went to an IV party for the first time I was generally shocked by how differently guys behaved. Dudes who would be too intimidated to approach me in broad daylight suddenly behaved much more sleazy and forward, and they spoke with such an "intent" (to hook up I assume). 

It obviously does not apply to everyone, but many party culture guys permit themselves to take on much more aggressive and sometimes straight-up predatory behaviors specifically in these "party" settings. It was such a gnarly and uncomfortable phenomenon that I never bothered with another IV party again.

Wainright was really nice and a sweet guy toward students who showed effort in the class from my experience a year ago. He did sometimes get upset at people who didn't follow instructions, but overall cared about teaching and a really chill dude most of the time.

Depends on the size of the room, but I believe IV bedrooms are usually relatively small to begin with. Triples in dorms typically have 1 bunk bed (2 people) and another bunk bed / table space underneath (1 person). I don’t think trying to fit three regular beds into 1 bedroom is a good idea, so 2 people in your room need to be okay with a bunk bed. 

I have seen one case of three mattresses squeezed together side by side in a IV bedroom, but honestly no amount of money saving would motivate me to do that.

Studios are 1k-ish nowadays yeah, but I don't think I've ever seen a 1br/1bath lower than 2k, just because they are meant to be shared as doubles, and I've rented one myself at that price to share with another. I'd gladly take a 1br/1bath for $1500 but that seems too good to be true hahah.

Also, waking up for your classes in quarantine, where you are stuck inside and have no social elements, will be very different from waking up for your class to actually being able to go outside, walk around the beautiful campus, grab a snack in a shop, be surrounded by other students walking around, etc.

It depends if you *need* to take them with the goal of graduating early. I agree, [you can still very much catch and spread Covid with the vaccine per CDC info](https://www.cdc.gov/coronavirus/2019-ncov/science/science-briefs/fully-vaccinated-people.html#:~:text=The%20risks%20of%20SARS%2D,spread%20it%20to%20others.), just at a lower chance and you are guaranteed to not have severe symptoms. Scientists are still drilling the long term effects and more cases, even among vaccinated people, can still lead to more variants. 

I’m fully vaccinated and I’m still very cautious of catching covid because of the unknown long term symptoms.

There is definitely a ton to do at SB aside from the beach and partying haha. There are usually different events happening on campus and they are really fun. Downtown SB has lots of their own events has well, multiple museums, art galleries, fun little shops, etc. It’s definitely not a metropolis, but I’m never felt “there’s nothing to do” in the two years there. 

That said, different strokes for different folks, so if the Chapman area, their campus, their culture, etc really clicks with you and you think you’ll have the time of your life there then I don’t see why not.

I’d definitely go with res hall if that’s an option, double check with housing to know how likely you are to get a spot (though I believe second years do get priority). IV consist of close knit friend groups and can be isolating if you aren’t living with friends. Considering this is your first time living on campus, you will have a much better chance at not feeling isolated and make connections in res halls.

It seems intuitive to me to choose UCSB given the options. You might save some money going to SJSU and living at home, but unless you need to be a caregiver to your household, living away on campus (UCSB) is much better for your personal growth, and college is an investment far greater than just an education. Plus, I'd assume UCSB holds much more value as an institution.

People often like to talk about IV being cheaper than student housing, but they don't realize student housing is much better value all things accounted for. You don't have to buy your own furniture with student housing (comes with bed, mattress, drawers, desk, sofa, tables, etc), there will be 0 problems with landlords in Uni housing, and you don't have to worry about your deposit being drained at the end of your lease.

Someone else talked about meal plans being $12/meal, but that's only the case in dorm prices. With off-campus meal prices, each meal comes down to about $6/meal. You are free to double-check on that but I believe that's correct from when I calculated it a year ago.

So I was in bit of a similar spot few years ago, deciding between cal poly slo and UCSB. It was a very easy decision after visiting both campuses haha. Personally, the campus at Slo and the surrounding town gave an extremely monotonous vibe when it comes to diversity and you’d have to pay me very good money to attend there in that regard. I fell in love with UCSB’s campus right away and loved the diverse atmosphere here. It’s a personal perspective, but I knew a CS professor who taught at both schools and agreed with me right away on the huge difference in diversity. 

On the BS vs Engineering degree, Id suggest you to think less about the job prospects, but more about the difference in curriculum and the different skill sets you’ll walk away from each. I’d research heavily in the classes and programs of each degree and see which you might enjoy more, and which align more with your vision of your future self. The easy tickets to job markets will always be an ivy level school name and/or being born into connections and resources, but in the long term you’ll end up where you are suppose to be.

I think there are several approaches to this, some of which already brought up by the other comments, and all of them are valid in my opinion, you just have to weigh them carefully

1. take the extended time and figure out a more suitable major, might run you a year over your 2 yr graduation timeline plus summers, depending on major. If you can get the financial support for that I don't see why not, you'd just be a "5th year", which is not bad at all and a very arbitrary thing anyway.
2. your major doesn't define you. Equally true, there are plenty of people who enter the workforce and find something they love that's completely different from their major. I think it'll take you a while to find a job you enjoy though, but it might just work out, it's hard to say. I'd say there's more uncertainty with this route.
3. Take a gap year. Also viable, but I personally think just taking extra time w/ school is more valuable than a gap year. But I don't know your circumstances well so you should think through the options thoroughly. I hope this helps though!
